summaries.example: Imagine you can promise to help a classmate with a project. You know that if you promise, you will later forget to help. If you do not promise, your classmate will find some help, though it may not be as good. One view says you should choose the promise because you could keep it. Another says you should not promise because you know what you would actually do. The debate asks which fact matters more: what you could do or what you would do.
summaries.summary: Actualism and possibilism are two ways of thinking about moral obligations. Suppose a person can begin a good plan, but would later freely abandon it. Possibilism says the person may still be required to begin if the complete plan is the best one they can perform. Actualism says the later failure matters, so another choice may be required if it would lead to a better result. The disagreement is not simply about whether the person has physical ability. Both sides may agree that the person can perform the whole plan in one sense. They disagree about whether that plan is a morally relevant option when the person cannot make sure it will happen. Philosophers have proposed middle views that consider what the person can secure or control, as well as ideas about primary and secondary obligations. The discussion began partly with questions about whether utilitarian rules fit together consistently, especially when a combined act is best but its separate parts seem to receive conflicting evaluations.
key_ideas: The debate asks which choices count when we decide what a person ought to do.
Possibilists focus on the best complete plan the person can carry out.
Actualists focus on what would really happen after each choice.
Neither view has been accepted by everyone; each faces difficult objections.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate helps us think carefully about responsibility, promises, planning, advice, and self-control. It asks whether moral rules should demand our best possible future or take our predictable behavior seriously. The answer can affect how we judge difficult choices without simply excusing bad behavior.

important_terms.definition: A moral rule about what someone is required to do.
A statement about what someone would do if a certain situation happened.
The view that what you should do depends partly on the best actions you could carry out over time.
The view that what you should do depends partly on what you would actually do after choosing it.

questions_to_think_about: Should we judge a choice by what a person could do or by what they would really do?
If someone can do something good but knows they will not finish it, should they begin?
Can two different choices both seem like obligations?
What advice would be helpful in the classmate example?

summaries.example: A professor is asked to review a student's paper. If she accepts, she can review it well, producing the best result, but she knows that she would later procrastinate and submit nothing. If she declines, the student receives weaker help but avoids the worst outcome. Possibilism says accepting can be obligatory because it begins the best complete series of actions the professor can perform. Actualism says declining can be obligatory because, given what she would do after accepting, declining leads to the better actual outcome. A securitist view asks whether the professor can secure the good series using intentions and attitudes that are permissible and presently available to her.
summaries.summary: The actualism/possibilism debate concerns how facts about an agent’s future free actions affect present moral obligations. In a standard case, an agent can begin a sequence whose ideal completion would produce the best result, yet would freely fail at a later stage. Possibilism gives moral importance to what the agent can do: an act is obligatory when it is part of the best maximal act-set available over the relevant period. Actualism gives moral importance to what the agent would do: an act is evaluated by the outcome that would in fact follow if the agent performed it. The disagreement therefore concerns the relevant set of alternatives and the relevant sense of “can,” not just ordinary physical ability. Historical discussion grew from attempts to formulate consequentialist principles without contradiction. A combined action can be best while its component actions appear to be individually best, producing tensions involving conjunction and implication. Actualist proposals differ over whether obligations are assessed step by step, relative to a context, or with control conditions. Possibilism avoids some conflicts but may appear to require acts that predictably lead to terrible outcomes. Actualism can reflect predictable wrongdoing but may let agents escape obligations because of bad dispositions or may recommend avoidable bad behavior. Securitist and related views try to hold fixed what is not presently under the agent’s control while preserving a strong role for agency. The entry also connects this debate with non-primary obligations and the maximalism/omnism dispute about whether non-maximal acts inherit their moral status from larger acts.
key_ideas: The central issue is which available alternatives are normatively relevant, not merely which actions are physically possible.
Possibilism evaluates an act through the best maximal act-set the agent can perform across time.
Actualism evaluates an option through the outcome that would follow from the agent’s actual future conduct.
Some actualist theories risk jointly unfulfillable obligations; procedural or contextual versions try to address this in different ways.
Possibilism faces the worry that it can require an initial act leading to a very bad outcome when failure is predictable.
Securitist, hybrid, and multiple-level theories seek positions between the two extreme views.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate tests basic assumptions about agency, responsibility, rational choice, and consequentialist ethics. It also affects formal principles about obligation, such as whether an obligation to perform a conjunction distributes to each component. More broadly, it asks how moral theory should respond when a person can do better in one sense but would predictably do worse in another. Because actualism, possibilism, and intermediate views can produce different advice and different judgments of responsibility, the issue matters for both ethical theory and practical deliberation.

important_terms.definition: The view that an act is obligatory when it belongs to the best complete series of acts an agent can perform over time.
The view that an option’s moral status depends partly on what would actually happen if the agent chose it.
A claim about what an agent would freely do under a fully described set of circumstances.
The moral status of an act as required, permitted, or forbidden.
A view that evaluates futures the agent can secure, while holding fixed facts not presently under the agent’s control.
An act-set that is not a proper part of a larger act-set available over the relevant period.
The principle that if someone ought to do A and doing A entails doing B, then they ought to do B.

questions_to_think_about: Does a predictable failure make an otherwise good plan cease to be a relevant option?
Can an obligation to perform a complete plan support obligations to perform each part of it?
Should moral advice track what is best in reality, even if the person cannot follow the advice?
Does treating moral and prudential decisions alike strengthen the case for actualism?
Which kind of control should matter when assessing future obligations?

summaries.example: Suppose Maya can sign up to tutor a younger student. If she signs up, she is capable of tutoring well, but she knows she would later skip the sessions. If she does not sign up, another tutor would help, but not as effectively. A possibilist might say Maya should sign up because she can be part of the best overall plan. An actualist might say she should not sign up because, if she does, the student would actually be left without the promised help. The question is whether “could tutor well” or “would fail to tutor” should guide the obligation.
summaries.summary: Actualism and possibilism offer rival accounts of how moral obligations depend on an agent’s possible future actions. Imagine that someone can begin a valuable plan but would later abandon it. Possibilism says the beginning may still be required because it belongs to the best complete course of action the person can carry out. Actualism says the beginning may not be required because the person’s later failure is part of what would happen if they began, and another option may have a better result. The disagreement is about morally relevant options. It is not necessarily a disagreement about whether the person has the ordinary ability to complete the plan. Philosophers also debate how to describe obligations over time. Some theories assess immediate choices first and then later choices. Others assess different groups of alternatives, which can create obligations that cannot all be fulfilled. Possibilism has the advantage of preserving rules that connect obligations to their consequences and parts, but it may require choices that predictably end badly. Actualism takes imperfect character and self-knowledge seriously, but critics say it can let people avoid good obligations simply because they are disposed to fail. Securitist and hybrid theories focus on what the agent can secure through suitable intentions and permissible attitudes. The broader discussion also connects to questions about conditional obligations, levels of obligation, and whether a smaller act gets its moral status from a larger act that includes it.
key_ideas: Actualists and possibilists may agree about what a person can physically do but disagree about which possibilities matter morally.
Possibilism looks at the best long-term plan the person can perform.
Actualism looks at the results that would follow from the person’s likely future behavior.
The views can give opposite answers in cases involving procrastination, weakness, or bad habits.
Critics worry that possibilism can demand a first step that leads to disaster, while actualism can excuse poor character.
Intermediate theories try to combine attention to control with attention to the best available future.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate gives us tools for examining promises, studying, teamwork, advice, and self-control. It shows why the same choice can look right under one moral theory and wrong under another. It also warns us that judging responsibility requires careful attention to time, intention, ability, predictable behavior, and the difference between an ideal plan and a secure one.

important_terms.definition: The idea that what someone ought to do depends on the best complete set of actions they can perform over time.
The idea that what someone ought to do depends partly on what would actually happen after they choose it.
A “would” claim about what an agent would freely do if a specified situation occurred.
A morally relevant choice or course of action among the options available to someone.
A moral requirement: something an agent is supposed to do.
A position that evaluates choices the agent can reliably secure, especially while setting aside facts outside present control.

questions_to_think_about: If you know you will abandon a plan, are you still obligated to start it?
Is it fair to judge someone by what they could do when their habits make success unlikely?
Should an adviser tell someone what is ideal or what will probably work?
Can a person have two obligations that cannot both be completed?
What should count as being in someone’s control?
